questions.question_text:
Which of the following depot formulations compares favourably with others listed in terms of symptom control but produces higher EPSE
burden?
questions.explanation:
Zuclopenthixol depot may be more suitable in aggressive patients. It may be better than other depots in relapse prevention though the
evidence in this regard is weak. EPSE burden is fairly higher with this depot.

questions.question_text: A male patient on clozapine has gained 20kg in 3 months though psychotic symptoms are well controlled. The next step is to:
questions.explanation:
This is an expected side e�ect, and the patient must be well informed beforehand. Lifestyle modi�cations help in most early cases, and this
must be the �rst intervention before altering the prescription.

questions.question_text:
A 45-year-old lady with a long-standing delusional disorder has now developed features of schizophrenia. She is poorly compliant with oral
antipsychotics and community nurse involved in her care suggests depot formulation. Which of the following is true concerning depot
antipsychotics?

options.text: Patients do not prefer depot medications consistently irrespective of previous exposure
The risk of tardive dyskinesia is equal for depot and oral formulation of same drug
The risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome is higher compared to oral drugs
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a contraindication for subsequent depot use
Atypical antipsychotics are not available in depot formulations.

correct_answer.text: The risk of tardive dyskinesia is equal for depot and oral formulation of same drug

questions.explanation:
The risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome is not higher for depot than oral drugs; reversibility may be poor in case of depots, if NMS
develops. There is no evidence to suggest that the neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a contraindication for subsequent depot use. Similarly
for the same drug, the risk of tardive dyskinesia is not higher for depot than oral formulations

questions.question_text: Which of the following is highly likely to be associated with both hyperglycaemia and dyslipidaemia ?
questions.explanation:
In the Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention E�ectiveness (CATIE) study, in which patients were randomly assigned to receive
olanzapine, perphenazine, quetiapine, risperidone, or ziprasidone, CATIE's phase 1 results showed that patients in the olanzapine group
gained more weight than patients in any other group, with an average weight gain of two pounds a month.

questions.question_text:
Nikolas is one of your patients with a primary diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. His brother is increasingly worried about Nikolas
committing suicide. Which of the following drugs has the best evidence for reducing suicidality in schizophrenia compared to others listed?
questions.explanation:
In terms of suicide prevention, the Intersept study compared clozapine and olanzapine. This was a 2-year multicenter RCT study comparing
the risk for suicidal behaviour in 980 patients with schizophrenia or schizoa�ective disorder treated with clozapine vs. olanzapine. Suicidal
behavior was signi�cantly less in patients treated with clozapine vs. olanzapine (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% con�dence interval, 0.58-0.97; P
=.03). Lithium may be a better choice in a�ective disorders.

questions.question_text:
A 22-year-old man presents with anxiety that his genitals are misshapen. He is not convinced in spite of a plastic surgeon reassuring him by
showing multiple images of normal genital appearances. Which of the following interventions has evidence-based support in the above
situation?
questions.explanation:
In a triple blinded RCT comparing e�cacy of �uoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder (40% patients had delusional BDD), �uoxetine was
increased by 20 mg/day every 10 days to a maximum of 80 mg/day. Signi�cant response started occurring after 8 to 12 weeks of treatment.
Patients who were delusional at baseline responded as well as non-delusional patients. Pimozide has only anecdotal evidence for
dysmorphophobic delusions and not preferred as the �rst choice drug due to QTc prolongation.

questions.question_text:
A 34 year old woman has an acute onset episode of intense suspiciousness and passivity phenomenon with auditory hallucinations. With
respect to the evidence based treatment of �rst episode psychosis which of the following is true?

options.text: No strong evidence in favour of lower antipsychotic doses
First generation antipsychotics are no better than placebo
Men and women respond di�erently to interventions in terms of resolution of symptoms.
Second generation antipsychotics are no better than placebo
RCTs show a clear di�erence between clozapine and other antipsychotics

correct_answer.text: No strong evidence in favour of lower antipsychotic doses

questions.explanation:
First and second generation antipsychotics (FGA and amp; SGA) are both better than placebo individually in treating acute psychosis. There
are no RCTs of clozapine in �rst episode patients. There is no evidence as to the correct mean dose for FGA drugs, but there is some
evidence for SGAs. There is no information about when to escalate or reduce dose. There is a limited evidence study that shows �rst-episode
patients require less medication. But there are no RCTs of �rst episode patients randomized to several doses. There is no evidence that a
lower dose is required for maintenance than for the acute episode. Gender di�erences are not noted in symptom management of �rst
episode psychosis (Retrieved from

questions.question_text:
A patient with unremitting continuous schizophrenic illness is considered for clozapine therapy. All of the following must be excluded before
initiating clozapine, except

options.text: High expressed emotions in the family
Dosage and duration of previous treatments

questions.explanation:
Factors other than choice of medication that may in�uence a patient's recovery include individual factors relating to the patient, the illness
and the treatment. Particularly relevant to the management of the incompletely recovered patient are poor compliance with medication,
concurrent illicit substance use (especially cannabis and psychostimulants), psychosocial stressors (eg, the home environment), physical
comorbidity (which may be secondary to treatment), associated organic abnormality, prominent negative symptoms and neuropsychological
de�cits.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following has been tried as an add-on therapy with antipsychotics for negative symptoms in patients with de�cit syndrome of
schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
E�cacy of add-on therapy with d-cycloserine, a partial agonist acting at the glycine modulatory site of the glutamatergic N-methyl-d-
aspartate receptor, was examined in 3 double-blind trials in patients with de�cit syndrome. 2 of the 3 studies suggest add-on d-cycloserine
50 mg/day may have some e�ect on negative symptoms in patients with de�cit syndrome despite small sample sizes and di�erent study
designs and duration. Glycine administration resulted in a signi�cant 30% 6 16% reduction (P and lt; 0.001) in negative symptoms in a study
wherein positive symptoms were also concurrently reduced. Selegiline was studied in a small number of patients in a 12-week placebo
controlled trial with some favourable results.

questions.question_text:
A 65-year-old lady with history of schizophrenia is not taking her medication. She is currently psychotic. When her son reminds her to take
her medications they end up having arguments. Which of the following medications is indicated?
questions.explanation: Depot medications are indicated in those with obviously poor compliance. Switching to clozapine may not help in this situation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following �rst generation antipsychotics was used in CATIE study?
questions.explanation:
CATIE stands for Clinical Antipsychotic Trials of Intervention E�ectiveness. The study design was a double-blind pragmatic RCT. In total, 1493
patients with chronic schizophrenia (mean duration of illness = 14 years) were enrolled across 57 sites from 2001 to 2004. Olanzapine,
quetiapine, risperidone, ziprasidone (added later in the trial) and perphenazine (only typical drug) were used in phase 1, and clozapine was
added in phase 2.

questions.question_text: Current clinical guidelines for management of schizophrenia support all of the following practices except

options.text: Depot can be used to help with adherence
Concurrent antipsychotic prescription must be tried only in �rst episode
No routine switch needed from typicals to atypicals
Treatment choice must be based on information sharing between patient and clinician
Consider clozapine as early as possible

correct_answer.text: Concurrent antipsychotic prescription must be tried only in �rst episode

questions.explanation:
According to NICE, the choice of antipsychotic drug should be made jointly by the patient and responsible clinician, on the basis of an
informed discussion of bene�ts and side-e�ects. Clozapine should be used at the earliest opportunity for patients with evidence of
treatment-resistant schizophrenia. "Atypical and typical antipsychotics should not be prescribed concurrently, except for short periods to
cover changeover of medication. If a patient on an oral typical has good symptom control and no unacceptable side-e�ects, a routine switch
to an atypical preparation is not recommended"( Retrieved from

questions.question_text:
A 44 year old man admitted in secure intensive care unit shows high degree of aggressiveness. He was diagnosed with schizophrenia 20
years ago. Which of the following medications has the best evidence in reducing aggression in schizophrenia compared to others listed
below?
questions.explanation:
A 12 weeks double-blind RCT compared clozapine, olanzapine, and haloperidol in high-risk patients with a history of aggressive behaviour.
Clozapine showed greater e�cacy than olanzapine and olanzapine greater e�cacy than haloperidol in reducing aggressive behaviour. This
anti aggressive e�ect appeared to be separate from the antipsychotic and sedative action of these medications.

questions.question_text:
The following scenarios depict �ve di�erent patients with schizophrenia. Which one of the following depiction is associated with a
comparatively positive prognostic outlook for schizophrenia?

options.text: Mr B had an acute onset psychosis at the age of 25. His family blames him for his own illness. He stays at a care home where the sta�
does not let him be with his family for more than 24 hours a week.
Mr A has predominantly negative symptoms and prefers to stay alone avoiding his friends who often urge him to go for walking trips
Mr C's major residual symptom is disorganised speech. On neurological examination shows grasp re�ex and dysdiadochokinesia.
Mr D had a very gradual and quiet onset of symptoms when he was 16 years of age.
Mrs C developed schizophrenia after getting married; her husband deserted her following the diagnosis.

correct_answer.text: does not let him be with his family for more than 24 hours a week.

questions.explanation:
Social isolation, living alone, having soft neurological signs and young onset are poor prognostic factors in schizophrenia. 'Expressed
emotion' was a concept originally developed by Brown and Rutter in 1966 as a part of the Camberwell Family Interview (audio-taped
interview with carer), and later modi�ed by Vaughn and Le� in 1976. The ratings are based on content and prosodic aspects and emphasis
of speech. Five measures are considered; 1. critical comments 2. positive remarks 3. emotional overinvolvement 4. hostility 5. emotional
warmth. A large amount of face-to-face contact (more than 35 hours per week) with a relative with a high expressed emotion score
increased the risk of relapse, but in households with a low expressed emotion score, high levels of contact appeared to be protective. Mr B is
somewhat protected as his contact is kept minimal by the care home sta�.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychosocial interventions has established evidence base in schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Psychosocial interventions in schizophrenia are aimed at improving functional outcomes and quality of life and not merely improving PANS
or SAPS scores. Psychosocial interventions are classi�ed as obligatory ones and voluntary ones by Bauml et al. The process of empowerment
of patients and their relatives to understand and accept the illness and cope with it in a successful manner is described as a basic-level
competency. This is considered to be an obligatory exercise upon which additional voluntary-exercise programs such as individual
behavioral therapy, self-assertiveness training, problem-solving training, communication training, and further family therapy interventions
can be built.

questions.question_text: Which of the following obstetric events are associated with increased risk of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Perinatal complications have stimulated interest as putative risk factors for schizophrenia. Low birth weight was initially implicated as a risk
factor; later anoxic brain damage at delivery was implicated, especially the dose of hypoxia was correlated to neuronal death. Kendell in
1996 showed that pregnancy induced hypertension increased the risk of psychosis almost 9 fold in a retrospective study design. Three
di�erent types of obstetric events have been described; 1. Growth related events e.g. low birth weight, small for gestational age 2. Perinatal
factors e.g. PIH 3. Hypoxic events e.g. premature rupture of membrane. Lewis-Murray scale has been speci�cally used to measure obstetric
complications during childbirth.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of simple schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Patients with simple schizophrenia show features of social and occupational decline, as well as negative symptoms in the absence of clear-
cut positive symptoms. Neuropsychological testing reveal evidence of general intellectual impairment plus de�cits in executive function and
memory.

questions.question_text: The single most important factor that increases risk of hospitalisation in the mentally ill is
questions.explanation:
Non adherence is the single most important factor increasing risk of hospitalization in the severe mentally ill (Weiden 2004, California
Medicaid data).

questions.question_text: In PANSS scale for schizophrenia, which of the following is coded as a positive symptom?
questions.explanation:
In PANSS, Conceptual disorganization is classi�ed under positive symptoms. Unusual thought content is classi�ed under 'General'
psychopathology

questions.question_text: What is the risk of schizophrenia in a child if both parents have schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
Genetic risk of schizophrenia decreases as one move from closer to distant relatives. If both parents have, schizophrenia the risk is around
40 to 50%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements best summarises the available evidence for treating cognitive symptoms associated with schizophrenia?

options.text: No conclusive evidence exists for the use of a speci�c agent against cognitive symptoms
These occur only in association with negative symptoms
These symptoms respond best to antidementia drugs
Amisulpride has the best evidence against cognitive symptoms in the absence of negative symptoms.
RCTs with paired observations accurately re�ect the cognitive improvement with atypicals.

correct_answer.text: No conclusive evidence exists for the use of a speci�c agent against cognitive symptoms

questions.explanation:
Cognitive symptoms occur independent of negative symptoms in schizophrenia. A number of studies have claimed cognitive bene�ts from
treatment with various second-generation antipsychotic drugs (SGAs). This claim is based on randomised comparative trials that
demonstrated that SGAs produce signi�cant improvement in neurocognition, measured by means of cognitive tasks administered at
baseline and follow-up assessments. Goldberg. et al 2007 designed a RCT of risperidone vs. olanzapine in patients with �rst-episode
schizophrenia, including a control group of individuals for whom data from multiple assessments were also collected. The main �nding was
that the e�ect size for cognitive change in patients exposed to SGAs was very similar to the e�ect size for cognitive change calculated in the
healthy control group. Hence cognitive improvements observed in RCTs may have been due to the non-speci�c e�ects of multiple testing
(practice e�ects).

questions.question_text: SSRI-induced sexual dysfunction occurs secondary to
questions.explanation:
Treatment with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) may lead to sexual dysfunction in up to 70% of patients. 5HT2 stimulation is
suspected to cause sexual dysfunction that may a�ect compliance with therapy and ultimately treatment success.

questions.question_text: Which of the following strategies has better e�cacy with respect to the administration of ECT?

options.text: Using sine wave instead of brief pulse ECT
Using unilateral instead of bilateral ECT
Using twice weekly instead of once weekly ECT
Using higher dose instead of lower dose of current

correct_answer.text: Using higher dose instead of lower dose of current

questions.explanation:
The UK ECT review group meta-analysis demonstrated that real ECT was signi�cantly more e�ective than simulated ECT. Premature
discontinuation happened equally in both real ECT and simulated ECT groups. Treatment with ECT (both B/L and U/L) was signi�cantly more
e�ective than pharmacotherapy (various drugs). Premature discontinuation was signi�cantly lesser in ECT than pharmacotherapy groups.
Bilateral ECT was more e�ective than unipolar ECT. But greater cognitive impairment was seen among patients treated with bilateral ECT. No
di�erence in e�cacy between twice a week and three times a week ECT, or between once a week and three times a week ECT, was noted.
High electrical dose led to a larger e�ect especially in bilateral ECT, but the e�ect was not signi�cant. But patients treated with high-dose
unilateral ECT took longer to regain orientation. No signi�cant di�erence in e�cacy was seen between brief pulse and sinewave ECT.

questions.question_text:
A community health worker regularly sees a patient with OCD. She wants to use a scale to screen for depression before asking the patient to
attend your clinic for an evaluation. Which scale would you choose?

options.text: Schedule for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry

questions.explanation:
A community health worker can screen for depression in a high-risk group by using self-rated Beck's depression inventory. Other scales
mentioned here may not be useful for the given clinical scenario. A trained clinician could use Hamilton Depression Rating Scale in OCD
patients to assess severity and presence of depression

questions.question_text: The highest risk of serotonin syndrome is seen in which of the following patients?

options.text: 55 year old taking phenelzine and escitalopram
67 year old taking amitriptyline and phenelzine
44 year old taking venlafaxine and mirtazapine

correct_answer.text: 55 year old taking phenelzine and escitalopram

questions.explanation: MAOI and SSRI combinations must be avoided at all costs as risk of fatal serotonin syndrome is substantial.

questions.question_text: You are treating 5 patients with depression in your outpatient unit. Which of the following patients is highly likely to drop out of treatment?

options.text: 26 year old who is a school drop-out
25 year old man with 3 previous depressive episodes
33 year old with more subjective than objective depression

correct_answer.text: 26 year old who is a school drop-out

questions.explanation:
In STAR*D trial, immediate attrition after one visit was associated with younger age, less education, and higher perceived mental health
functioning. Attrition later in treatment (but within 12 weeks) was associated with younger age, less education, and African American
ethnicity. Experience with more than one episode of depression was associated with less attrition.

questions.question_text:
A GP writes to you asking clari�cation regarding depression treatment guidelines. Which of the following practice, if employed, is not
recommended?

options.text: He uses SSRIs as �rst line drugs
In case of comorbid anxiety and depression, he treats anxiety �rst.
In mild depression, if patient agrees, he does not do much apart from o�ering 2 weeks follow up.
He classi�es depression according to symptom count
He does not give antidepressants to those with mild depression at �rst consultation.

correct_answer.text: In case of comorbid anxiety and depression, he treats anxiety �rst.

questions.explanation:
In cases of comorbid depression and anxiety, depression must be managed initially. Depression must be classi�ed as per severity for proper
management. Watchful waiting with no active intervention for mild depression is an advocated strategy if agreeable; review must be in 2
weeks.

questions.question_text:
A patient being treated with antidepressants for long loses faith in the treatment and asks you if antidepressants really work. Which of the
following is an accurate response?

options.text: They work if one takes them for at least 4 months.
They work in moderate depression though with increasing severity they lose e�cacy
They work well for adults though not so well for the elderly.
They work best for young children as they take them regularly
One additional response occurs for every 5 depressed adults who take antidepressants

correct_answer.text: One additional response occurs for every 5 depressed adults who take antidepressants

questions.explanation:
In adults NNT for antidepressant response seems to be 4-5; for remission it may be 6-7 for short term trials (around 12-14 weeks). In elderly
it is found that the NNT for tricyclics is 4; 8 for SSRIs and 3 for MAOIs. In children and adolescents NNT for SSRIs was of uncertain clinical and
statistical signi�cance; paroxetine had NNT bene�t 12 (5 to ) and NNT harm 20. Sertraline had NNT bene�t 10. Fluoxetine had somewhat
clinically worthwhile NNT bene�t of 5 (4-13).

questions.question_text: With respect to the programmes intended to prevent depression which of the following is true?

options.text: Targeting high risk groups is profoundly e�ective compared to non speci�c strategies of prevention
Programmes with single focussed methods are more e�ective
Multicomponent programmes are better than single component programmes
Programmes with social intervention has the best e�ect for working age adults
Depression cannot be prevented in older age groups.

correct_answer.text: Multicomponent programmes are better than single component programmes

questions.explanation:
Depression prevention programmes that included three or more di�erent types of methods were signi�cantly better than those that
included only one or two. Programmes that involved a competence enhancement component yielded the largest e�ect sizes, whereas
programmes including behavioural methods yielded the lowest e�ect sizes. For older age group social support programmes yielded larger
weighted e�ect sizes. No di�erence in e�ectiveness was found between universal, selective and indicated programmes - hence targeting
high-risk groups only may not o�er any speci�c advantage ( no cost analysis was done). Jane-Llopis E, Hosman C, Jenkins R, et al. Predictors
of e�cacy in depression prevention programmes: a meta-analysis. Br J Psychiatry 2003;183:384-97

questions.question_text:
A patient living in rural Scottish highlands has an episode of depression. Despite her husband's insistence she refuses any intervention or
treatment. How long would her depressive episode last?
questions.explanation: An untreated depressive episode lasts 6 to 13 months; most treated episodes last about 3 months.

questions.question_text: The median duration of a treated episode of depression is
questions.explanation: An untreated depressive episode lasts 6 to 13 months; most treated episodes last about 3 months.

questions.question_text:
A depressed patient is a keen naturalist. He wants to try a herbal remedy for depression. What would you choose from the following
options?
questions.explanation:
An initial meta-analysis of St Johns Wort (Hypericum perforatum) published in 2001 showed an adjusted RR of 1.94 (1.5 to 2.5) in favour of
SJW. But when 3 later studies were added, and the data was re-analysed, this e�ect size dropped to 1.30 (1.0 to 1.60). In fact, SJW may not be
as e�ective as once claimed. Evidence from at least one systematic review of multiple well-designed RCTs are found for the use St John's
wort, tryptophan/5-hydroxytryptophan, S-adenosyl methionine, inositol and folate in depressive disorders. None of these �ndings was
conclusively positive, and folate had a signi�cant e�ect only when combined with an antidepressant.

questions.question_text:
A psychiatrist diagnoses depression using ICD10 criteria in a 24-year-old lady who attends her outpatient clinic. Which of the following
diagnosis is she highly likely to receive if subsequently followed up for several years?
questions.explanation: A diagnosis of depressive disorder is the most likely diagnostic outcome in patients with a �rst episode of depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antiepileptics causes visual �eld defects?
questions.explanation:
Wilton at al reported an increase in the number of con�rmed cases of visual �eld defects attributed to vigabatrin in their observational
cohort study. Ref: Wilton et al., BMJ. 1999;319:1165-1166

questions.question_text:
A known bipolar patient has had many episodes of mania but no clinically signi�cant depression so far. But currently he presents with
severe depression. He is already on lithium with good serum levels and is compliant. What will be the next step?
questions.explanation:
Treatment with an antidepressant [SSRI] together with a mood stabiliser is recommended for severe depression. Gijsman et al.( 2004) found
that symptoms were nearly twice as likely to improve in patients who received an antidepressant than in those who received placebo or a
mood stabilizer alone.

questions.question_text:
A 45-year-old woman has recurrent depression and hypomanic episodes which occur only when she is treated with ECT. She has had 4
episodes of ETC-induced hypomania in the past. Which of the following terms provides the most accurate description of her illness?
questions.explanation:
The term bipolar III is sometimes used for recurrent depression, plus hypomania occurring solely in association with antidepressant or other
somatotherapy. Bipolar IV refers to depression superimposed on a hyperthymic temperament.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has RCT evidence in favour of treatment during acute episodes of mania?
questions.explanation:
RCTs in people with bipolar type I disorder experiencing a manic episode suggest that clonazepam may be as e�ective as lithium in
improving manic symptoms at 1 to 4 weeks. But guidelines do not recommend it as monotherapy.

questions.question_text:
A 44 year old patient has been admitted 7 times with a relapse of bipolar disorder in last few years. Which of the following laboratory
investigations is very important in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Rapid cyclers have higher rates of current hypothyroidism. A poor response to lithium (especially the depressive component) is also
associated with rapid cycling

questions.question_text:
A known bipolar patient has had many episodes of mania and depression so far. He also had signi�cant episodes of manic switch following
SSRI treatments in the past. Currently he presents with severe depression. He is already on lithium with good serum levels and is compliant.
What will be the next step?
questions.explanation:
Quetiapine at either 300 mg/day or 600 mg/day is more e�ective than placebo at treating depression in people with bipolar I or II disorder
(Geddes, 2003).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most important predictor of relapse in a patient with bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation:
Perlis et al. (STEP-BD) found that the biggest predictor of relapse was residual symptoms, and the majority of relapses were into depression.
Index phase may have a bearing on relapse and overall outcome. Patients with a depressive index phase spent the highest proportion of
time being ill (65% of time nearly), especially with depression in both bipolar 1 and 2 types. Patients with a manic index phase spent the
smallest proportion of time ill (30% time nearly), especially in depressive states (n= 191, 18m follow up. Mantere et al, 2008).

questions.question_text:
A 35 year old lady is going to be discharged from hospital after successful treatment of a depressive episode. She has had 5 depressive
episodes in the past and this time following depression she developed hypomania. What would you prescribe?
questions.explanation:
Note that this woman was hospitalised and is getting discharged now. NICE recommends using long term maintenance treatment - after a
manic episode involving signi�cant risk and adverse consequences, in bipolar I disorder with two or more acute episodes, and in bipolar II
disorder with signi�cant functional impairment or risk of adversities. Lithium monotherapy is the �rst line treatment. It is probably e�ective
against both manic and depressive relapse, although it is more e�ective in preventing mania.

questions.question_text: In comparing bipolar depression with unipolar depression all are true except:

options.text: A family history of bipolar disorder is more common in bipolar depression.
There are some notable phenomenological di�erences
Antidepressant induced hypomanic switch suggests bipolar disorder
Psychotic depression in earlier adulthood is suggestive of bipolar disorder
Atypical symptoms are more common in unipolar depression

correct_answer.text: Atypical symptoms are more common in unipolar depression

questions.explanation:
Notable but subtle phenomenological di�erences have been reported. Atypicality is in favour of bipolar depression. Higher family history of
bipolar disorder suggests bipolar depression; presence of psychotic depression in early adulthood is also suggestive of bipolar disorder.
Anxiety, insomnia and somatic complaints are more in unipolar depression.

questions.question_text: Median time to recover from a treated episode of mania is
questions.explanation: Median time to recover from mania (treated) is around 4-5 weeks.

questions.question_text:
A 24-year-old man has been using amphetamines for the last six months. He had an episode of depression when he was 22; this was
treated by his GP using �uoxetine. He now presents with euphoria, increased energy and activities with psychotic features suggestive of
mania. He was admitted and remains drug-free for six weeks now. However, his symptoms have continued without change. The most
appropriate diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
In stimulant or other street drugs induced mania, if the mood state signi�cantly outlasts the drugged state then a diagnosis of bipolar
disorder can be made.

questions.question_text: Which of the following prodromal symptoms is more suggestive of schizophrenia rather than bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation:
In a prospective study of prodromal features in those with high risk of bipolar, it was noted that the prodrome was predominantly insidious
(greater than 1 year) in more than half of the patients; acute presentations with less than 1 month of prodrome were very rare; subacute
was more common than acute but less common than insidious prodromes. The prodrome duration did not di�er between those with
psychotic and nonpsychotic mania. Attenuated positive symptoms and increased energy/goal-directed activity were signi�cantly more
common in the prodrome of patients with later psychotic mania. Mania and schizophrenia prodrome characteristics overlapped
considerably. However, subsyndromal unusual ideas were signi�cantly more likely part of the schizophrenia prodrome;
obsessions/compulsions, suicidality, di�culty thinking/communicating clearly, depressed mood, decreased concentration/memory,
tiredness/lack of energy, mood lability, and physical agitation were more likely part of the mania prodrome.

questions.question_text:
A 36 year old man treated for bipolar disorder wants to know which drug can prevent suicidal behaviour in bipolar patients. The best option
is
questions.explanation:
For hospital admitted patients, the suicide risk is around 10% over long-term follow-up. Based on naturalistic comparison of patient cohorts,
the �ndings from di�erent centres. Consistently report that lithium could have a suicide prevention e�ect. The treatment e�ect is very large
for this �nding. (Geddes 2003).

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is most likely to cause hyponatraemia?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine is more likely than the others listed to cause SIADH, resulting in euvolemic hyponatremia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the diagnostic stability of bipolar disorder is true?

options.text: The diagnosis of bipolar disorder is delayed in those with index depressive phase
More patients lose than retain a diagnosis of bipolar disorder
Bipolar 1 to bipolar 2 switch happens frequently.
Bipolar 1 diagnosis is less stable than bipolar 2.
After 5 years of symptom free period, a diagnosis of bipolar can be removed.

correct_answer.text: The diagnosis of bipolar disorder is delayed in those with index depressive phase

questions.explanation:
Approximately 40% of patients with bipolar disorder get misdiagnosed previously as having unipolar depressive disorder initially. But once a
diagnosis is made the stability of bipolar disorder has generally been reported to be high, ranging from 70% to 91%. In bipolar disorder,
bipolar I is more stable than bipolar II just because bipolar II may switch to bipolar I, but not vice versa.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants is highly likely to induce a mood switch from depression to mania?
questions.explanation:
Antidepressant-induced mania is known as mood 'switch'. This is a short-term phenomenon and takes place soon after starting
antidepressants. It is more commonly associated with tricyclics.

questions.question_text: All of the following are contraindications for zopiclone except
questions.explanation: Though zopiclone can rarely increase amnesic tendency, having memory impairment is not a speci�c contraindication for this drug.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to generalized anxiety disorder?

options.text: Concordance of DZ twins more than MZ

questions.explanation:
The feature of avoidance is not needed for diagnosis; GAD is often punctuated by depressive episodes and co-existent with a number of
comorbid diseases.

questions.question_text: With regard to PTSD which of the following is true

options.text: Chronic pain is associated with PTSD.
Resilience is not a dynamic quality
Prevalence of PTSD is the same all over the world
Prior trauma does not increase susceptibility to PTSD

correct_answer.text: Chronic pain is associated with PTSD.

questions.explanation:
PTSD is probably underdiagnosed. Resilience to traumatic experience is a dynamic quality and same person may respond di�erently to
traumatic exposures at di�erent times. Prevalance of PTSD is high in regions of civil unrest and war. Chronic pain is associated with PTSD

questions.question_text:
With respect to the recommended treatments for PTSD which of the following are endorsed by NICE guidelines for use in primary care
settings?
questions.explanation: Paroxetine, mirtazapine are endorsed by NICE for general use; amitriptyline or phenelzine for specialist use in PTSD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neuroimaging �ndings is most consistent with OCD?

options.text: Decreased metabolism at dorsal prefrontal cortex

questions.explanation:
Many investigators have contributed to the hypothesis that OCD involves dysfunction in a neuronal loop running from the orbital frontal
cortex to the cingulate gyrus, striatum (cuadate nucleus and putamen), globus pallidus, thalamus and back to the frontal cortex. Organic
insult to these regions can produce obsessive and compulsive symptoms. The results of neurosurgical treatment of OCD strongly support
this hypothesis. Surgical interruption of this loop by means of cingulotomy, anterior capsulotomy or subcaudate tractotomy brings about
symptomatic improvement in a large proportion of patients unresponsive to all other treatments. FMRI shows increased orbitocingulate
metabolism in OCD.

questions.question_text:
A 20-year-old man is sent home from college as he was drunk before giving a presentation. He is reported to be spending more time alone
as his friends have stopped calling him due to his repeated refusals to go out with them anymore. He is refusing to go to a family meal for
his father's birthday as he says he would be so tense that he may vomit at the party. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
It is important to note that the bulk of evidence to date suggests that alcohol rarely, if ever, reduces social anxiety. Nearly all studies of
clinical individuals with social phobia and normal comparison subjects confronting socially frightening stimuli fail to �nd alcohol anxiolytic.
Clearly, these results con�ict with the popular perception that alcohol is a social lubricant by virtue of its ability to reduce anxious distress in
social situations. In fact, most patients presenting with social phobia present with comorbid alcohol problems.

questions.question_text: In PANDAS which of the following tests is most likely to be positive?
questions.explanation:
In PANDAS the neuropsychiatric symptoms need not have their onset during a streptococcal (group A beta-hemolytic) infection; only an
exacerbation that correlates temporally with the infection is also acceptable for a diagnosis. AntiDNAseB or Antistreptolysin O titres are
likely to be elevated in most with recent streptococcal infection. A fraction of these may have auto antibodies to neurons in basal ganglia (
the so called anti basal ganglia antibodies). These are not established as diagnostic of PANDAS though initial studies are encouraging.

questions.question_text: In PTSD there is con�rmed e�ectiveness for all of the following treatments except:
questions.explanation: Hypnotherapy is not indicated and has no evidence base to support its use in PTSD.

questions.question_text: In the aetiology of PTSD choose one correct option:

options.text: locus of control has no role
the sympathetic nervous system is not involved
unresolved childhood trauma increases the risk.
lower level of education is protective

correct_answer.text: unresolved childhood trauma increases the risk.

questions.explanation:
Hippocampus is implicated in functional MRI of PTSD patients. Patients with PTSD may have disturbances in locus of control (externalising
the possibility of further trauma). Lower educational level increases susceptibility. Overactive sympathetic system is suspected. Unresolved
childhood trauma may predispose to vulnerability for PTSD.

questions.question_text:
A 44 year old man with generalised anxiety wants to try a herbal remedy for his anxiety. He is not worried about the side e�ects. Which of
the following would be an option?
questions.explanation:
Herbal treatment of anxiety: The kava shrub (Piper methysticum) has been studied in anxiety disorders. The e�ects of kava are due to the
kavapyrones, which in animal models act as muscle relaxants and anticonvulsants, protect against strychnine poisoning, and reduce limbic
system excitability. They may cause inhibition of voltage-dependent sodium channels, increase GABAA receptor densities,
blocknorepinephrine reuptake, and suppress the release of glutamate. Several double-blind, placebo-controlled trials have shown kava to
be more e�ective than placebo in reducing HAM-A scale scores and this e�ect is detectable even within 1 week of therapy. Kava is
associated with allergic, sometimes fatal hepatotoxicity and so not recommended for general use. (Beaubrun and Gray, 2000)

questions.question_text: OCD which of the following symptoms may be speci�cally resistant to treatment?
questions.explanation:
Compulsive hoarding may be a neurobiologically distinct form of obsessive-compulsive disorder. Hoarding is notoriously di�cult to treat by
either psychological or pharmacological means. Symmetry obsessions tend to be chronic and treatment resistant.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true with regard to the diagnostic criteria for an acute stress reaction?

options.text: Symptoms diminish or resolve only if the stressor is removed
Symptoms start after 48 hours of exposure to stressful event

questions.explanation:
An acute stress reaction follows a sudden severe stressor and lasts for only a few days. By de�nition, an acute stress reaction occurs in an
individual without a previous psychological disorder.

questions.question_text: The �rst line treatment in an adult with severe OCD is

options.text: A choice of either SSRI or CBT

correct_answer.text: A choice of either SSRI or CBT

questions.explanation: According to NICE a choice must be o�ered between drugs and CBT, with a view of combining them in due course.

questions.question_text: Which of the following outcomes is often used to de�ne treatment response in OCD treatment trials?

options.text: YBOCS scores fall below detectable levels

questions.explanation: 'Response to treatment' after 6 - 12 weeks of treatment is de�ned as a fall of at least 35%  in the pre-treatment YBOCS score.

questions.question_text: Many patients with chronic fatigue syndrome will meet the criteria for
questions.explanation:
Many patients with CFS will meet the criteria for another psychiatric diagnosis, most commonly major depression. Arguments exist for
calling CFS a form of atypical depression; however this is untenable in a signi�cant minority of cases. Not only do patients resist a psychiatric
diagnosis, but many do not have anhedonia or pervasively low mood and attribute any mood disturbance to the restriction on their activities
caused by their illness. Nonetheless, treatment of comorbid depressive or anxiety symptoms can produce clinical improvement. Ref: Oxford
Handbook of Psychiatry; 2nd ed: Pg 754

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with restless leg syndrome can present with periodic limb movements during sleep?
questions.explanation: Up to 80% to 90% of RLS patients can present periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS).

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is not a diagnostic criterion for restless leg syndrome?

options.text: Distressing, irresistible need to move legs usually accompanied by paresthesias

questions.explanation:
RLS presents the following four diagnostic criteria in patients aged 12 or older: Akathisia (distressing, irresistible need to move legs), usually
accompanied by paresthesias. (This is a core feature), Motor restlessness, Symptoms worsen at rest and Symptoms worsen at night. It is a
neurological sensorimotor disorder characterized by unpleasant sensations in the legs that preclude a smooth transition from wakefulness
to sleep. These symptoms can also signi�cantly interfere with personal or social activities. Patients will have excessive daytime sleepiness.
The prevalence of RLS to be from 3% to 15% of the general population (median 7.2%). M:F = 1:2 ( twice as prevalent in women as in men).

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a core feature to make a diagnosis of restless leg syndrome?

options.text: Distressing, irresistible need to move legs

correct_answer.text: Distressing, irresistible need to move legs

questions.explanation:
RLS presents the following four diagnostic criteria in patients aged 12 or older: Akathisia (distressing, irresistible need to move legs), usually
accompanied by paresthesias is a core feature. Others include Motor restlessness, Symptoms worsen at rest and Symptoms worsen at
night.

questions.question_text: In REM sleep behavioural disorder, the associated lesions are situated in which part of the brain?
questions.explanation:
Rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is thought to result from a dysfunction of the brainstem structures that regulate
physiologic REM sleep muscle atonia

questions.question_text: The �rst-line treatment for Restless Leg syndrome is
questions.explanation:
Pharmacologic treatment options for RLS include dopaminergic agents (l-dopa, pergolide, pramipexole), anticonvulsants (gabapentin, CBZ),
opioids (oxycodone, propoxyphene), and clonazepam. The drug �rst licensed was ropinirole; however, several other medications have been
used "o�-label" for years. Benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) have been used with moderate success, but there is concern regarding
potential for dependency to these drugs.

questions.question_text: Which one among the following is a maintaining factor for CFS?

options.text: Attributing the illness to physical cause

correct_answer.text: Attributing the illness to physical cause

questions.explanation:
Patients with CFS strongly believe in physical cause of CFS and refute role of psychological and personal factors. This leads to increase in
symptoms and reduces in level of functioning Patients with CFS are sensitive to stimuli arising inside the body (introspection) and perceive
activity as an e�ort. They believe that they are seriously ill .This leads to avoidance of activities which in turn perpetuate the illness. The
inactivity is caused by perceptual distortion rather than physical �tness. They also fail to estimate their cognitive abilities and studies have
shown di�erence between actual and perceived cognitive performance.

questions.question_text: Which is the most common presenting symptom of obstructive sleep apnoea?
questions.explanation:
Obstructive sleep apnoea: It is more common in men (4%) than in women (2.5%). History of loud snoring, breathing pauses, mouth
breathing, restless sleep, and increased perspiration at night. Snoring is the most common presenting symptom. Other symptoms include
excessive daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, and behavioural changes (paradoxical hyperactivity or depression, anxiety, emotional
lability). Right sided cardiac failure may occur in the untreated.

questions.question_text:
Mr. X su�ers from recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterized by a panicky scream, with intense fear. He has no recall
of the details of the event and is unresponsive during the episode. His most likely diagnosis is;
questions.explanation:
Night terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterized by a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic
arousal. The individual usually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive during the episode. Night terrors occur during
the �rst third of the night, during stages 3 and 4 of NREM sleep.

questions.question_text: Initial insomnia is frequently related to which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Initial insomnia is characterized by di�culty falling asleep, with increased sleep latency. It is frequently related to anxiety disorders. Middle
insomnia refers to di�culty maintaining sleep. It is associated with medical illness, pain syndromes, or depression. In terminal insomnia or
early morning wakening, patients consistently wake up earlier than needed. This is frequently associated with major depression.

questions.question_text: Which neuropeptide has been found to be low in patients with narcolepsy?
questions.explanation:
Hypocretins (Orexins) are hypothalamic neuropeptides believed to play a role in regulating sleep and arousal. Abnormally low
concentrations of hypocretin-1 (Orexin-A) have been found in the CSF of patients with narcolepsy.

questions.question_text: Identify the good prognostic factors of CFS from the list given below.

options.text: Patients not attributing CFS to physical causes.
Belief in complete rest as the treatment

correct_answer.text: Patients not attributing CFS to physical causes.

questions.explanation:
Good prognostic factors include a lack of strong attribution to physical causes, less severe baseline fatigue, and younger age (Children and
adolescent recover faster). Poor prognostic factors include psychological comorbidity, a strong belief in physical cause for CFS, a belief that
complete rest is therapeutic, presence of severe fatigue at presentation, older age and a longer illness duration.

questions.question_text: Which immunological test is diagnostic of CFS?

options.text: Increased expression of activation markers on the surface of T lymphocytes
De�ciency in natural killer cell function
Increased number of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells bearing antigenic marker

questions.explanation:
Evidence for immune system abnormalities is inconsistent. No immunological test is diagnostic of CFS. Only few abnormalities have been
consistently reported after extensive research Increased expression of activation markers on the surface of T lymphocytes Increased
number of CD8+ cytotoxic T cells bearing antigenic marker . De�ciency in natural killer cell function The abnormalities suggest low level
immune activation but its signi�cance is unclear. Interleukin 6 may play an important role in CFS as it is involved in stress response and
sickness behaviour

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is classi�ed as a dyssomnia?
questions.explanation:
Dyssomnias are primary sleep disorders which cause either di�culty getting o� to sleep or remaining asleep (insomnia) or excessive
sleepiness during the day. They are divided into Primary insomnia, Primary hypersomnia, Circadian sleep disorders, Narcolepsy, Breathing
related sleep disorders and Sleep state misperception. Parasomnias (disorders which intrude into the sleep process) are subdivided
according to the phase of sleep with which they are associated: Arousal disorders (Confusional arousals, Sleepwalking, Sleep terrors), Sleep-
wake transition disorders (sleep starts, sleep talking etc), REM sleep parasomnias (REM behavioural disorder, Nightmares, Sleep paralysis).
There are also other parasomnias are those which do not fall into these three categories such as Sleep bruxism and Sleep enuresis

questions.question_text: Diagnostic features of neurasthenia include all of the following except
questions.explanation:
CFS criteria US-CDCP (1994) suggests that to diagnose CFS (or neurasthenia in ICD10), patients must have persistent or relapsing
unexplained chronic fatigue. The fatigue must last for at least 6 months and should appear not to be alleviated by rest.

questions.question_text: The most common problem seen in patients with medically unexplained symptoms is the potential for
questions.explanation:
A problem common to all patients with medically unexplained symptoms is the potential for iatrogenic harm. These patients often accrue
considerable morbidity and even mortality due to excess negative investigations, irradiation, operative procedures, etc. Those disorders
associated with chronic pain carry the risk of iatrogenic opiate dependency. Often at the later stages of the patient's illness this secondary
morbidity is more problematic than the original symptoms. A major positive intervention in these patients is therefore the avoidance of
iatrogenic harm. Ref: Oxford Handbook of Psychiatry; 754

questions.question_text: Which of the following modes of treatments is not endorsed by evidence-based guidelines for managing anorexia?
questions.explanation: While CBT and CAT have a modest evidence base to support their use, IPT or DBT do not have any supportive evidence for anorexia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of emotionally unstable personality disorder?
questions.explanation:
Impulsive traits with a high degree of emotional instability and fear of abandonment is seen in emotionally unstable/borderline personality
disorder.

questions.question_text:
A 28-year-old man comes to your outpatient clinic who has been arrested 8 times in the past for hitting his girlfriends. He had 10 previous
relationships. He is now starting a new relationship and is worried that the same will happen again. As a child he has a history of truancy,
hitting other children and getting into trouble with police for drinking. Your examination reveals no indication of a current mental illness.
What would you do?

options.text: No medication as he has no treatable illness
Prescribe antidepressant to prevent psychiatric disorders.
Prescribe an anti-psychotic and follow up in the clinic
No medication but follow up as he is at higher risk of psychiatric disorders

correct_answer.text: No medication but follow up as he is at higher risk of psychiatric disorders

questions.explanation:
The diagnosis is antisocial PD. Given that he has no mental illness now, prescribing lithium, antipsychotic or antidepressants is not
warranted. Patients with antisocial PDs have a high risk of mental illness, and the patient here is undergoing a life event (starting a new
relationship). It will be necessary to o�er a follow up at the least.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not commonly associated with bulimia?
questions.explanation:
Repeated binges and vomiting result in oesophageal tears, dental erosion. Seizures may occur due to repeated vomiting and resulting
electrolyte imbalance. Parotid enlargement is secondary to repeated vomiting and salivary secretion. Peptic ulcer is not directly related to
bulimia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a laboratory abnormality seen in anorexia?
questions.explanation:
Low concentrations of leutenising hormone, follicle stimulating hormone, and oestradiol, Low T3, T4 in low normal range, normal
concentrations of thyroid stimulating hormone (low T3 syndrome), mild increase in plasma cortisol, raised growth hormone concentration,
severe hypoglycaemia (rare), low leptin (but possibly higher than would be expected for bodyweight), hypercholesterolaemia, raised serum
carotene are some of the abnormalities seen in anorexia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cluster of personality disorders is most commonly seen in psychiatric outpatient samples?
questions.explanation: In psychiatric OPD samples a distribution of the following pattern is noted: Cluster A = 6% Cluster B = 13% Cluster C = 22% Any PD = 46%

questions.question_text: Monozygotic concordance rate in anorexia is estimated to be around
questions.explanation:
For anorexia nervosa, monozygotes have 55% concordance and dizygotes have 0 to 5% concordance. For bulimia nervosa, monozygotes
have 35% concordance and dizygotes have 30% concordance.

questions.question_text:
A patient with mixed personality disorders show predominantly low mood, temper outbursts, dysphoria and recurrent suicidal behaviour.
Which of the following could be prescribed based on the symptom pro�le?
questions.explanation:
For a�ective dysregulation symptoms in PD a trial of SSRIs may be useful though there is no evidence base to support this in regular
practice.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are common physical features seen in anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation:
Cardiac e�ects from anorexia nervosa include profound bradycardia, hypotension, decreased the size of the cardiac silhouette, and
decreased left ventricular mass associated with an abnormal systolic function(Anorexia Nervosa - Medscape Reference. (n.d.). Retrieved
from

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true concerning the diagnosis of eating disorders?

options.text: Anorexia is more prevalent than bulimia
Most patients with anorexia have a past history of bulimia
A typical binge can include 1000-2000 Cal
Binge episodes are characteristic of anorexia
Anorexic patients seek treatment more often than bulimic patients

correct_answer.text: A typical binge can include 1000-2000 Cal

questions.explanation:
Binge is more often seen in bulimia, can include up to 1000-2000Cal food. Bulimics seek treatment more than anorexics. History of anorexia
is common in those with bulimia the vice versa is not that frequent but well recognised.

questions.question_text:
A patient presents with impulsive nature and anger outbursts that has led to several criminal charges. Which of the following would be an
appropriate diagnosis when considering personality disorders?
questions.explanation:
Antisocial personality disorder is also known as dissocial personality disorder. It is associated with lack of regard for the rights and feelings
of other people and a high degree of impulsivity.
